newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan plans to cut vegoil imports by half.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan plans to cut vegoil imports by half.

text.p: Pakistan plans to cut vegetable oil imports by half in the next two years by increasing domestic production, Finance and Economic Affairs Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Saturday .
"We plan to cut edible oil imports by half in the next two years," he told Reuters after addressing businessmen and industrialists.

Pakistan's edible oil imports fell 19.65 percent to 583,111 tonnes worth $319 million in the first eight months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) compared to 725,703 tonnes worth $586 million in the year-ago period.
Edible oil imports included 497,269 tonnes of palm oil worth $271 million, mainly from Malaysia.
Vegoil dealers attributed the fall to higher production of domestic edible oils.
"The main thrust of the government is to increase agricultural production," Aziz said.
The rise could be six to seven percent, Aziz said and added "You will see a dramatic change in our economy."

The government will focus on agriculture and industry as without a substantial growth in agriculture, wheat and cotton Pakistan will not be able to increase its exports, he said. "Without an increase in agricultural production our balance of payments will not be covered."

New Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government announced two packages last month to increase agricultural and industrial production and exports. Several taxes and customs duties were cut to help industry.
"Our target is to double exports in three years from the present about $9.0 billion," Aziz said. "The exports will be increased by higher production."

Earlier, Aziz told the meeting that the new government was business-oriented and market-friendly and its approach would reduce Pakistan's dependence on loans from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
"We have lowered taxes to revive the economy and restore industrial competitiveness," he said. "The whole atmosphere has to be changed. We want to introduce a new business culture."
